source.title: Scaling Laws vs Model Architectures : How does Inductive Bias Inﬂuence Scaling? An Extensive Empirical Study on Language Tasks
source.authors: Yi Tay; Mostafa Dehghani; Samira Abnar; Hyung Won Chung; W. Fedus; J. Rao; Sharan Narang; Vinh Q. Tran; Dani Yogatama; Donald Metzler

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present, including main results and appendix.
record.tranche_reason: It runs scaling sweeps and fits performance-versus-scale slopes across architectures, testing scaling behavior with a different model and setup from the original decoder-only studies.
record.gate_note: The paper reports validation perplexity and fitted slopes for multiple architectures, plus depth- and width-scaling comparisons. Table 1 checkpoint-level scores are not separately cataloged because the fitted architecture-level slopes and scaling-protocol comparisons are the reported results most directly bearing on these versions. The paper cites other scaling studies, but cited findings are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study trains 10+ encoder-decoder architectures (16M–30B params) on C4. It fits slopes of upstream negative log-perplexity and fine-tuned downstream accuracy against FLOPs and parameters, testing whether scaling behaviour holds across architectures (a new setting). It does not reproduce the decoder-only power-law fits.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Authors also claim the vanilla Transformer has the best scaling (highest α), though Table 2 shows higher values for Universal (αP,U) and Switch (αU,D). They warn that novel inductive biases, especially attention changes like Performer and Mixer, are risky at scale.
record.recipe_differences: Uses multi-architecture encoder-decoder models trained on C4 with a shared setup; it fits architecture-specific slopes and examines depth/width protocols rather than reproducing the original decoder-only scaling-law setup.
record.method_sensitivity: Architecture and scaling protocol (depth versus width) change scaling behavior; upstream and downstream trends can differ.

fits_no_version.finding: Scaling protocol (depth vs FFN width) for MoS, Transformer, Evolved and LConv: upstream trends are similar across protocols. On downstream, depth scaling has a much larger effect than width.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Scaling protocol (depth vs width) affects downstream transfer scaling more than upstream loss scaling.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are reported for fitted slopes. Comparisons use a shared training recipe and do not test token-count scaling or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. The authors caution that the largest Switch model was scaled sub-optimally. Depth/width results are presented in figures without extracted numeric values.
record.rows_left_out: None. Table 2's five fitted coefficients for each of 11 architectures and the reported depth- and width-scaling comparisons are included.

untested.parts: Power-law functional form: only linear slopes on (apparently log) axes, no exponent or fit quality. Token/data scaling: all runs use a fixed 2^19 steps. Range is about two orders of magnitude, not 'several'.
No extrapolation from small to large runs.
No comparison of depth/width at fixed parameter count. Depth and width sweeps change size.
Text only. No power-law test for fine-tuning loss or other modalities; downstream is accuracy.
Parameter-counting conventions, schedules, data, and fitting method are not systematically varied.

missing.what: Per-checkpoint upstream losses showing curves flattening or reversing at the top: Switch XL worse than Large (-1.62 vs -1.56), LConv flat Large→XL (-1.76 vs -1.75), Performer plateau.
Universal Transformer: raising recurrent steps increased FLOPs but did not improve performance.
Same-size cross-architecture losses, e.g. at ~220M: Transformer -1.75, Performer -2.23, LConv -1.95, MoS -1.70. Relevant to V4 only under a broad 'architecture details' reading.

record.verdict_notes: The 'slope of a fitted linear line' is never defined (axes appear log-scaled for scale and linear for negative log-perplexity), so it is not a power-law exponent, and there are no uncertainties. Table 2's caption mislabels the αP,U column as (F,U). The fixed 2^19-step training means token count is never varied. ALBERT spans only 15M–34M and Universal only up to 283M. Authors flag the largest Switch model as sub-optimally scaled. Tranche changed to T3: a new architecture setting, not the same question by a different method.

versions.untested_parts: The paper evaluates upstream validation perplexity against parameter count and FLOPs, not token-count scaling; it does not establish prediction over several orders of magnitude from these fits alone.
No prediction from small runs to substantially larger runs is reported.
No fixed-compute optimization of the parameter/token allocation is conducted.
The depth/width comparisons do not establish that these shape changes have only slight effects at a fixed parameter count.
No other modality or test of whether the same loss power law holds under repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer is reported.
Downstream results are reported for GLUE, SuperGLUE, and SQuAD; the study does not establish a general predictive law for all downstream tasks.

The study shows architecture-dependent fitted slopes and scaling behavior, but does not systematically vary parameter-count conventions, fitting methods, or training schedules, nor establish curves bending away from a power law.

source_check.notes: All 22 listed numerical values and model ranges match the source. The main correction is claim alignment: Table 2's linear slopes support architecture-dependent scaling descriptions, but do not establish V1's power-law form or V7's exponent dependence.

statements.correction: Shared C4 training; architecture-dependent upstream scaling; Table 2 reports fitted linear performance slopes, not loss power-law exponents. Other numerical examples in this statement concern other studies.
